title: One Word to Explain America
text:
I n May 2020 , as COVID-19 besieged America, Jim Justice, then the Republican governor of West Virginia, held a televised press conference. “I encourage all businesses that are allowed to open to do so only if they fuckin’ follow the guidelines to keep West Virginians safe,” he said. Social-media users across the nation were quick to celebrate, or mock, the governor’s directive. Justice swiftly claimed that the bad word in question was the result of an audio glitch, calling it a “word that I would never say nor have I ever said.” It was a technical difficulty, not a human one. Now you hear it; now you don’t.

 Justice may in fact have stumbled verbally , resulting in an inadvertent F-bomb. Either way, the subsequent hoopla marked a revealing and absurd crossroads in the history of American English. For many Americans, purity of tongue remains a benchmark of godliness, decency, and social order. Bad words symbolize the opposite: corruption and shame and a symptom of national distress. There are 21st-century American voters who still wash out their children’s potty mouths with soap. Justice’s denial nodded to decorum, without rejecting those West Virginians who liked his edginess. Whether or not voters remembered or cared about the governor’s gaffe, or his about-face, they elected him to the Senate in 2024.

 Americans have always cursed. But Americans have also always opposed cursing. That paradox is baked into the nation’s origins. The earliest American colonists brought with them from England a robust stream of earthy, impious, and provocative words. They also imported strong countervailing taboos against the use of those words. Many national cultures and their linguistic codes are built out of such contradictions, as verbal-rule breakers try to defy or evade the so-called word police—figures of religious, political, or economic authority bent on silencing shameless tongues and stopping wanton pens from scribbling.

 In today’s United States, curse words are more deeply embedded in public conversations than ever before. Politicians, especially the current occupant of the Oval Office, have rewritten the rules of modern public rhetoric. This spring, on Easter Sunday, President Trump shared a message to Iran’s leaders on Truth Social: “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in hell.” Three months earlier, Mayor Jacob Frey had invited ICE to “get the fuck out of Minneapolis.” Whether they love to use them or hate to hear them, Americans have always associated improper words with social lowness. Yet today, “low” words keep becoming more popular as a means for proclaiming how bold and rebellious we want to believe ourselves to be—even for the very authorities others rebel against.

 P rofanity across languages follows fairly consistent patterns, including sexual and scatological epithets as well as slurs directed at outside groups. But different cultures also have unique forms of cursing. In some places, for example, mentioning an ancestor who is supposed to remain unnamed counts as a profane outburst. Even languages such as Japanese and Finnish, sometimes reputed to be too tidy or repressed to include such terms, turn out to have their own impolite phrases for venting rage, exasperation, and mockery.

 [ Read: The case for mindful cursing ] 

 Most of our history of swearing is lost forever, borne away on the winds that scattered rude words far and wide. “To a great extent, the history of spoken language is a history written on water,” the scholar E. J. White has observed. What has survived is a disparate and fragmentary stream of documents—trial transcripts, diaries, private letters, crumbling newspaper articles, and yellowing novels. And many “bad” words come and go over time. Take Jim Justice’s use of fuckin’ : Colonial Americans spoke and wrote that word as a blunt but not profane gerund referring to sexual intercourse. It took quite some time for it to emerge in usage as an indecent but perversely honest adverb. A colonist in 17th-century Virginia or Massachusetts would have been puzzled, but not outraged, by the governor’s use of the word to urge his fellow citizens to obey public-health measures. In turn, the profane exclamations that those colonists might have blurted out to underscore an emergency of catastrophic proportions—“cud’s buds” or “zounds!” ( God’s body or God’s wounds! )—would elicit head-scratching from Justice’s 2020 audience.

 The English sense that such outbursts are attached to a certain baseness has survived the cultural twists and turns of more than four centuries in America. To early colonists, the human body itself was seen as proof of that lowness. According to some European Christian perspectives, the “higher” faculties of the mind and senses were concentrated in the head, nearer to heaven. Meanwhile, the shameful or foul functions of sexual appetite, urination, and defecation were lodged farther down, and therefore nearer to hell. Adjectives such as mean were used to describe those at the bottom of the socioeconomic ladder: peasants, laborers, beggars, and bandits. These classes were associated with sin, vice, and crime, as well as sinful, vicious, and illicit speech. By contrast, godly, polished, elevated speech belonged to the elite realms of monarchs, nobles, wealthy merchants, learned professionals, and their kin, who could afford the time and education to master it.

 Accordingly, in the U.S. as in England, profane, rude, and filthy language became a stigma. To use it was to join the distasteful masses. The exceptions proved the rule: Wealthy or middle-class men or women who flouted the norms of decent speech and behavior were seen as living beneath themselves. Or so innumerable sermons, lessons, and etiquette books had it.

 A funny thing happened on the way to modernity: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, as the Great Migration brought rapid cultural changes to major American cities and as younger generations flouted Victorian prudery, bad words began to be seen as rebellious and ironically good. To use them became a way of signaling brash new American identities and tastes. Their positive worth came to reside precisely in their lowness, their coarse frankness, and, crucially, their public airing. Improper words and censorship have something of a symbiotic relationship: If they weren’t forbidden, curse words wouldn’t be potent or satisfying to say.

 As hard-boiled veterans, blues divas, jazz musicians, and their ilk took on more prominent roles in American culture, dirty words, with newly positive connotations of sass and bluntness, became part of an irreverent new American style in self-presentation and conversation. For many Americans, “low-down” words revitalized expression. They made everyone feel like an outlaw, in a good way. They broke through phoniness to reality. That sea change is still with us every time we use a four-letter word and, for a brief moment, channel our inner badass. It’s why, even if you wince at the statement “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards,” you can probably also sense the purpose of Trump’s profanity: It projects a peculiarly American form of confidence and defiance of inherited conventions.

 [ Read: Politicians aren’t cool enough to curse this much ] 

 Using bad words can be part of a pose, or a calculated ploy to signal spontaneity. Today, they often project edginess and daring. They have also come to represent the wordscape of our post-privacy culture, an ecosystem of would-be influencers in which we are unwilling or unable to keep our impulses from guiding how we present ourselves. If you want to get a non-presidential sense of how messy things have become in our current age, just go online and read some of the squabbles between parents who upload cute videos of their cursing tots and those who slam that practice as disgraceful.

 These flame wars might be entertaining, but they also hint at how much the politics of cursing continue to change. Social and technological developments have turned the question of who can use certain hot-button words—and in what contexts—into a minefield. If a mom gets called “bitch” in the comments section on Instagram, it can be read as wildly insulting or proudly affirming. After Representative Ted Yoho, a Republican, allegedly called Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez a “fucking bitch” in 2020, she denounced “violent language against women” from the floor of the House, while also tweeting , “But hey, ‘b*tches’ get stuff done.” Whether the word was bad-bad or bad-good depended on who used it and how. But in both of these cases, the risky choice of language comes from one source: It’s the danger of these words, and the common urge to police them, that gives them their seductive and persistent power.

 This article was adapted from Steven H. Jaffe’s new book, Four-Letter Nation: The Long, Dirty History of American Profanity .
